title: 3D Atlas: Redi’s Three-Jar Controlled Experiment
question: Why do maggots appear only on meat that adult flies can physically touch, even when air circulates freely through fine gauze?
explanation: Rotating Redi’s three glass jars in 3D shows that the gauze-covered jar admits scent and oxygen while blocking adult Sarcophaga flies, proving that maggots hatch from laid eggs rather than arising spontaneously from decaying meat.
limits: Displayed fly trajectories and larval growth rates are scaled for visual clarity.

title: 3D Atlas: Hooke & Leeuwenhoek Optical Bench
question: How did a tiny single glass bead lens outperform larger early compound microscopes to reveal living bacteria?
explanation: Exploding the brass paddle and cork specimen stage in 3D shows how Leeuwenhoek’s short-focal-length spherical glass bead achieved 270× magnification with ~1.3 µm resolution, whereas Hooke’s two-lens compound tube magnified cork cell walls at ~30×.
limits: Chromatic and spherical aberrations are summarised via the Rayleigh resolution limit.

title: 3D Atlas: Pasteur’s Swan-Neck Gravity Trap
question: How does a curved glass neck allow oxygen in while keeping boiled nutrient broth sterile for years until tilted?
explanation: In the 3D swan-neck flask, airborne dust and bacterial spores settle by gravity into the lowest U-bend of the glass tube. Only when you tilt the flask past 42° does sterile broth wash into the bend and carry trapped microbes back into the bulb.
limits: Spore settling is modelled as deterministic trapping at the lowest bend.

title: 3D Atlas: Eleven Orders of Magnitude of Life
question: Why must we switch from the naked eye to light microscopy and then electron microscopy as we zoom from a blue whale down to a DNA helix?
explanation: Sweeping the logarithmic 3D scale dial across eleven orders of magnitude compares specimen dimensions against the wavelength of visible light (~400–700 nm), showing why viruses and ribosomes require electron beams.
limits: Organism and macromolecule meshes are shown normalized inside the 3D comparison stage.

title: 3D Atlas: Seed Hydration and Development
question: How does adding water change a viable seed, and what can a hydration model establish?
explanation: Inspect a schematic chickpea cutaway. Chosen hydration parameters illustrate swelling and possible development; water enters permeable coat regions.
limits: Illustrative rates and opening threshold, not measured seed data. Added-water percentage is relative to starting seed mass, unlike the chapter workbench water fraction.

title: 3D Atlas: Candle Combustion vs Seed Metabolism
question: How do cellular pathways connect fuel reactions to ATP regeneration and construction?
explanation: Compare a conceptual flame account with coupled cellular reactions. Both involve reaction networks; only the cell has the coordinated machinery for cellular maintenance and inheritance.
limits: The standard-state ATP allocation is a chosen account, not measured cellular efficiency or heat. Drawn steps do not count reactions.

title: 3D Atlas: ATP Reactions and Cellular Work
question: How can an ATP reaction be coupled to movement or chemical construction?
explanation: Inspect the ATP schematic and rotary synthase. ATP reactions can support work when enzymes connect them to other changes; bond breaking alone requires energy.
limits: Symbolic molecular representation. Whole-reaction free energy depends on conditions; an isolated bond does not contain the reaction free-energy change.

title: 3D Atlas: ATP Supply and Cellular Work
question: How does ATP connect energy transfers to cellular processes?
explanation: Inspect the ATP carrier and rotary ATP synthase. Gradient-driven synthesis regenerates ATP; other enzyme systems couple ATP reactions to cellular work.
limits: The rotor represents one ATP-synthesis mechanism, not all seven life processes or a literal gear connection between them.

title: 3D Atlas: Why Viruses Require a Host
question: What cellular machinery does a virus lack for independent replication?
explanation: Compare the viral capsid and bacterial host. Host ribosomes make viral proteins; enzymes copy the genome, using resources of the infected cell.
limits: One schematic phage-host interaction. Other viruses enter differently; the capsid geometry is chosen, and absence of independent metabolism does not mean all chemistry stops.

title: 3D Atlas: Representative green plant cell
question: How do the wall, vacuole, nucleus, mitochondria and chloroplasts fit together?
explanation: Inspect the selected plant-cell structures in solid, X-ray and section views. A white onion bulb cell lacks developed chloroplasts while retaining mitochondria.
limits: Schematic selected structures and counts; not every real plant cell has this equipment.

title: 3D Atlas: Organelle ancestry clues
question: Which observations support bacterial ancestry for mitochondria and chloroplasts?
explanation: Compare membrane folds and stacks with inherited DNA and bacterial-related ribosomes described in the chapter. Gene comparisons supply evidence beyond appearance.
limits: Shapes alone do not establish ancestry; fold-area gain is a chosen geometry model.

title: 3D Atlas: Cell geometry and a chosen surface layer
question: How does enlarging a cube change its surface area relative to volume?
explanation: Change cube width and compare SA/V=6/L with the inner core remaining beneath a chosen 5 µm surface layer.
limits: The coloured core is geometric, not measured oxygen penetration or a universal starvation limit. Assumed diffusion coefficient 2000 µm²/s; differs from chapter centimetre-block example.

title: 3D Atlas: Specialised cell shapes
question: How do thin regions and extensions support different cell functions?
explanation: Inspect a biconcave red blood cell, root hair and myelinated neurone. Relate their different shapes to exchange and communication.
limits: Selected schematic shapes, not a vesicle-trafficking simulation or universal measured area gains.

title: 3D Atlas: Membrane diffusion and equilibrium
question: Can opposing molecular crossings continue when net transfer is zero?
explanation: Compare a lipid boundary and chosen equal-volume relaxation model; molecules continue moving near equilibrium.
limits: Schematic particles and invented rate constant; not atomic dimensions or measured flux.

title: 3D Atlas: Water-selective channel
question: How can a protein provide a faster water route without pumping it?
explanation: Inspect a schematic hourglass channel and two-way exchange markers. Compare total water potentials for the direction of net transfer.
limits: Not atomic coordinates, calibrated molecular throughput or a full map of selectivity chemistry.

title: 3D Atlas: Animal and plant water relations
question: Why can a supporting wall change the outcome of water entry?
explanation: Compare schematic red-blood-cell and walled-cell states as external solute conditions change. Pressure contributes to total water potential.
limits: Chosen qualitative state thresholds and swelling scales, not universal cell-specific predictions.

title: 3D Atlas: Illustrative energy-coupled carrier
question: How can an ATP-dependent carrier sustain transport that passive spreading would not?
explanation: Inspect a generic carrier cycle and chosen ATP-response curve. The chapter separately explains root nitrate uptake through an ATP-built proton gradient and cotransporter.
limits: Not Skou’s sodium–potassium pump or a real root nitrate pump. Chosen uncharged-solute ratio omits electrical forces; ATP loss need not instantly remove stored gradients.
